specPoints.text: understand how to use dot-and-cross diagrams to represent covalent bonds in: diatomic molecules, including hydrogen, oxygen, nitrogen, halogens and hydrogen halides; inorganic molecules including water, ammonia and carbon dioxide; organic molecules containing up to two carbon atoms, including methane, ethane, ethene and those containing halogen atoms.

primer.text: From the earlier note in Covalent Bonding you know that a covalent bond is a shared pair of electrons between two non-metal atoms. This note puts that idea on paper: dot-and-cross drawings for the small molecules the exam names, from hydrogen and the halogens through water, ammonia and carbon dioxide, up to methane and its two-carbon relatives.

lessons.title: Diatomic molecules
lessons.opening: Diatomic molecules contain exactly two atoms, and their dot-and-cross diagrams are the simplest covalent drawings. Hydrogen shares one pair, chlorine shares one pair, oxygen shares two pairs and nitrogen shares three. Hydrogen chloride follows the hydrogen pattern, with one pair shared between a hydrogen atom and a halogen atom.
keyPoints: A diatomic molecule contains exactly two atoms, such as H2, Cl2, O2, N2 or HCl.
Hydrogen and the halogens form single covalent bonds, so one pair is shared in each of H2 and Cl2.
Oxygen shares two pairs, giving a double bond, and nitrogen shares three pairs, giving a triple bond.
Hydrogen chloride shares one pair between the hydrogen atom and the halogen atom.
Each shared pair in the drawing uses one electron from each atom, keeping the donor symbols visible.

low.restatement: Draw each atom's outer electrons with its own symbol, then overlap the shells where the sharing happens. Hydrogen and chlorine overlap once for a single bond, oxygen twice, and nitrogen three times; every overlap is one shared pair, which is one covalent bond.
low.analogy: Think of two lockers sharing a shelf: the shelf holds books from both owners at once, and the more shelves the two lockers share, the stronger the connection between them.
low.examPointer: Count pairs carefully in the exam: one overlap for single bonds, two for oxygen, three for nitrogen, and state the number of shared pairs if asked.

medium.restatement: The diagrams encode bond order visually: one overlapping shared pair for hydrogen, the halogens and the hydrogen halides; two for oxygen's double bond; three for nitrogen's triple bond. Each atom contributes one electron per shared pair, so the donor symbols remain traceable inside every overlap.
medium.analogy: Picture brackets holding two shelves together: one bracket for a light load, two for a heavier one, three for the heaviest, mirroring single, double and triple bonds.
medium.examPointer: If a question asks how many electrons are shared in O2, multiply the two bonds by the two electrons in each pair to reach four.

check.stem: How many shared pairs does a molecule of nitrogen, N2, contain?

options.explanation: Nitrogen shares three pairs between its two atoms, the largest count among the common diatomic molecules.
One pair would suit hydrogen or chlorine; nitrogen needs three pairs to complete both outer shells.
Two pairs belong to oxygen's double bond; nitrogen shares one pair more.
Five pairs is beyond any molecule in this course; nitrogen shares exactly three.

check.stem: In the dot-and-cross diagram for hydrogen chloride, what is shared?

options.text: One electron pair, one electron from the hydrogen and one from the chlorine
options.explanation: The single bond of HCl is one shared pair with one donor electron from each atom.

options.text: A pair of electrons both donated by the chlorine
options.explanation: Each atom contributes one electron to a normal covalent bond; neither atom donates the whole pair.

options.text: All seven of chlorine's outer electrons
options.explanation: Only one of chlorine's outer electrons enters the bond; the other six stay non-bonding.
Hydrogen and chlorine are both non-metals, so they bond covalently by sharing.

check.stem: How many electrons are shared in total in a molecule of oxygen, O2?

options.text: Four, because oxygen forms two covalent bonds and each bond carries one shared pair
options.explanation: Two shared pairs means four shared electrons in total across the double bond.

options.text: Two, one from each atom into a single pair
options.explanation: Two shared electrons would be one single bond; oxygen shares two pairs.

options.text: Sixteen, all of the electrons present
options.explanation: Only the four bonding electrons are shared; the remaining electrons stay non-bonding on their own atoms.
Eight would be four pairs; the oxygen molecule carries exactly two shared pairs.

check.stem: Which diatomic molecules are named in the spec for this diagram skill?

options.text: Hydrogen, oxygen, nitrogen, the halogens and the hydrogen halides
options.explanation: The spec lists these diatomic families for dot-and-cross practice, alongside the named inorganic and organic molecules.
The halogens are one family on the list; hydrogen, oxygen, nitrogen and the hydrogen halides are named too.

options.text: All diatomic molecules in the Periodic Table
options.explanation: The requirement covers the named families, not every diatomic possibility.
The full list runs from hydrogen through nitrogen, the halogens and the hydrogen halides.

check.stem: What does one covalent bond always represent?

options.explanation: The exam hint states it directly: each covalent bond is one shared pair, whatever the molecule.
Two pairs make a double bond, which is a specific case such as oxygen, not the general bond.
Transfer belongs to ionic bonding; covalent bonds share a pair.
The equivalence is fixed: one bond, one pair, two electrons.

lessons.title: Inorganic & organic molecules
lessons.opening: The inorganic molecules on the list share pairs between unlike atoms: water has two single bonds, ammonia has three, and carbon dioxide has two double bonds. The organic drawings extend the same skill to carbon skeletons of up to two carbon atoms, covering methane, ethane, ethene and the halogen-substituted versions.
keyPoints: Water shares one pair in each of its two O-H bonds, and ammonia shares one pair in each of its three N-H bonds.
Carbon dioxide shares two pairs with each oxygen atom, making two double bonds in the molecule.
Methane has four single C-H bonds, and ethane adds a C-C single bond between its two carbon atoms.
Ethene contains a C=C double bond, two shared pairs between its two carbon atoms.
Organic molecules in scope contain up to two carbon atoms, including versions with halogen atoms attached.

low.restatement: Water joins one oxygen to two hydrogens with one pair each; ammonia joins one nitrogen to three hydrogens; carbon dioxide joins one carbon to two oxygens with two pairs each. The organic set repeats the pattern around carbon chains of one or two atoms.
low.analogy: It is like assembling toy molecules with two-peg joints and four-peg hubs: hydrogen offers one peg, oxygen two, nitrogen three, and carbon four, so the shared pegs show exactly which bonds form.
low.examPointer: Draw every outer electron, then mark the shared overlaps; examiners check that both the bonding pairs and the non-bonding electrons are visible.

medium.restatement: Each central atom donates as many shared pairs as its bonding pattern demands: oxygen two, nitrogen three, carbon four. The inorganic set exercises unlike-atom sharing, while the organic set, capped at two carbon atoms, adds carbon-carbon single and double bonds and halogen substitution without changing the pair-sharing principle.
medium.analogy: Think of carbon as a four-socket adapter, oxygen a two-socket one and nitrogen a three-socket one; the molecule is complete when every socket of every atom is filled by a shared pair.
medium.examPointer: Ethene is the classic double-bond check: two pairs between the carbons, two hydrogens per carbon, and four shared pairs across the whole molecule.

check.stem: How many covalent bonds does one molecule of ammonia, NH3, contain?

options.text: Three, one between the nitrogen and each hydrogen
options.explanation: Each N-H link is one shared pair, and the molecule carries three of them.
One bond would join nitrogen to a single hydrogen; the formula NH3 names three hydrogens.
Four bonds would suit methane's carbon; ammonia's nitrogen bonds to three hydrogens.
Two bonds would leave one hydrogen unattached; the three hydrogens each need a bond.

check.stem: What is the bonding in carbon dioxide, CO2?

options.text: Two double bonds, one between the carbon and each oxygen atom
options.explanation: Carbon shares two pairs with each oxygen, and the two oxygens are otherwise unconnected.
Single bonds would leave carbon two pairs short of its four-bond pattern.

options.text: One double bond between the two oxygen atoms
options.explanation: The oxygens bond to the carbon, not to each other; carbon sits at the centre.

options.text: A triple bond and a single bond
options.explanation: The pattern at this level is two identical double bonds; mixed bond orders do not appear here.

check.stem: Which organic molecules must you be able to draw dot-and-cross diagrams for?

options.text: Methane, ethane, ethene, and organic molecules containing halogen atoms, up to two carbons
options.explanation: The spec caps the organic list at two carbon atoms and includes the halogen-substituted versions.
Longer chains sit beyond the stated cap of two carbon atoms.
Methane is the smallest example; ethane, ethene and halogenated molecules are named too.
Rings with more than two carbons fall outside the two-carbon cap.

check.stem: How many shared pairs surround the carbon atom in methane, CH4?

options.text: Four, one pair with each hydrogen
options.explanation: Carbon's four bonding pairs are each shared with one hydrogen, completing every outer shell.
Two pairs would leave two of carbon's four bonds unformed.
Eight pairs would mean sixteen shared electrons; methane carries four pairs.

options.text: None, the hydrogens bond to each other
options.explanation: The four hydrogens each bond to the central carbon, not to one another.

check.stem: Ethene, C2H4, contains a carbon-carbon double bond. What does that mean for the shared electrons?

options.text: Two pairs, four electrons, are shared between the two carbon atoms
options.explanation: A double bond is two shared pairs, so four electrons join the carbons.
One pair makes a single bond, as in ethane; ethene's carbon link is double.
Three pairs would be a triple bond, which belongs to nitrogen among the named molecules.
Four pairs exceed any bond in this course; a double bond carries exactly two.

glossary.definition: Describing a molecule made of exactly two atoms.
A bond formed when two atoms share a pair of electrons.
Two shared pairs of electrons between the same two atoms.
Three shared pairs of electrons between the same two atoms.
A group of atoms joined by covalent bonds, acting as a single unit.
